FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE Contact: A shley B rittain, 858-204-0756 Office of House Majority Leader Jason Monks, R-Meridian Legislature's Tough Decisions and Accurate Forecasting Delivered Idaho's Strong Fiscal Finish, Monks Says BOISE, Idaho — House Majority Leader Jason Monks (R-Meridian) today credited the Idaho Legislature's disciplined budgeting, accurate revenue forecasting, and willingness to make hard decisions for the state's strong close to Fiscal Year 2026. "Idaho finished the year strong, and Idahoans deserve to know why," Monks said. "It wasn't luck, and it wasn't a press release. It was the Idaho Legislature doing the hard, unglamorous work of budgeting — setting a realistic revenue number, making difficult spending decisions, and passing a balanced budget as the Idaho Constitution requires. Credit belongs where the work was done: in the people's branch of government." When lawmakers convened in January, Idaho faced a projected budget shortfall. Rather than kick the can down the road, the Legislature acted early and decisively. The Joint Finance-A ppropriations Committee adopted its revenue projection on just the eighth day of the 2026 session — compared to day 59 the year before — giving budget writers a firm, realistic foundation from the start. The Legislature's forecast proved remarkably accurate. When the books closed on Fiscal Year 2026, final General Fund collections came in approximately $19.2 million above the Legislature's forecast — while finishing roughly $171.9 million above the executive branch's revised forecast. On a General Fund of more than $5.5 billion, the Legislature's estimate landed within a fraction of one percent of actual collections. "When your forecast is within one-third of one percent of reality, that's not just a guess," Monks said. "The Legislature's number was the one the budget was actually built on, and it held up." A ccurate forecasting alone didn't balance the budget. Legislators made the difficult votes to right-size state government, approving budget reductions for most state agencies and programs to guard against revenue uncertainty and prevent the state from running a deficit. Those decisions were not easy or popular, but they were necessary — and they worked. Idaho ended the fiscal year with a positive cash balance that allows the state to carry roughly $250 million into next year's budget.

"Every one of those votes had a name attached to it," Monks said. "One hundred and five legislators went home to their neighbors and explained why we tightened the state's belt. That's what accountability looks like, and that's why Idaho finished strong." Key accomplishments this session included holding K-12 education funding harmless, a substantial pay raise for the Idaho State Police, and new tax relief on tips and overtime through conformity with the B ig B eautiful B ill — approximately $155 million this year and $175 million next year. That relief comes on top of roughly $4 billion in tax cuts delivered over the last five years. Monks emphasized that the Legislature will bring the same discipline to the upcoming session. "We'll keep doing what we did this year: forecast honestly, spend within our means, and pass a balanced budget. That's not one man's accomplishment — it's the Legislature's constitutional duty, and we'll keep delivering on it."
